body:
Priya: Quick follow-up from yesterday's RFC — can we agree on where RBAC checks live for dashboard tile queries? I sketched two options and want tradeoffs before the spike.

Tom: +1, we should decide before we make routing changes. TL;DR: option A = enforce at query-router (single gate), option B = enforce at materializers (distributed).

Lena: For SLOs I'd prefer option A — single place means easier caching and cheaper preflight checks. But single gate is a perf hotspot unless we shard.

Marco: Option B is friendlier to scaling: each materializer can check tenant perms locally and short-circuit. Downside: duplicated policy logic and harder to patch policy bugs.

Olga: Security note: duplicated logic increases risk of inconsistent policy rollout. We can mitigate with a small shared policy lib + feature flag. Also audit logs get messy if checks are spread.

Tom: Thoughts on hybrid? Router does coarse-grained checks (canReadDashboard) and materializer does fine-grained row-level checks when needed. Router can also attach a short-lived auth token to traffic.

Priya: Hybrid sounds promising. How would that affect prefix caching and tile reuse?

Marco: If router guarantees the dashboard-level allow, materializers can keep optimistic prefix caches keyed by (tenant, dashboard_id). We won't need to validate every cache hit if router attaches the signed token. Token TTL should be tiny (30s).

Lena: Perf question: generating signed tokens per request adds CPU — do we benchmark? Maybe sign once per routing decision and reuse for batched tile requests.

Tom: Proposed config snippet for token header:
```yaml
headers:
  x-rd-auth-token: "signed:ttl=30s;tenant=123;dash=456;sig=..."
```
Router asserts signature, materializers verify signature only, not policy logic itself.

Olga: That reduces policy duplication but we still need materializer-level verifications for sensitive widgets (column-level masking). For those, materializers fetch policy and enforce. So hybrid + selective deep-check.

Priya: Ok so final design: 1) Router does coarse allow + attaches signed short-lived token. 2) Materializers accept token for fast-path; deep checks for sensitive tiles. 3) Central policy service for sensitive checks + audit logs. 4) Feature-flag rollout.

Tom: I'll open a follow-up RFC PR with diagrams and perf targets. Need numbers: target p95 addl latency for router signing < 5ms, token verify in materializer < 1ms.

Lena: I'll schedule a microbenchmark: signing QPS 2k/s and 10k/s to see CPU impact. Also test cache hit ratio changes when using optimistic token reuse.

Marco: Implementation note: use our existing crypto lib (fast-hmac) and keep tokens compact to avoid header blowup. Also add middleware in materializer for token cache to avoid repeated crypto calls for same token in a batch.

Olga: I'll prepare the audit schema changes (need to record router decision, token id, materializer verification result).

DeployBot: New RFC follow-up created: https://go/internal/rfcs/console-routing-tokenized-auth — reviewers: @Tom @Olga @Lena @Marco.

Priya: Great, thanks all. Let's sync Friday for the spike plan. :thumbsup:
